newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan retaliates for Cambodia move, assails China.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan retaliates for Cambodia move, assails China.

text.p: Taiwan on Monday severed its unofficial ties with Cambodia and assailed arch rival China as a "black hand" that was deliberately damaging what had been Taipei's strong economic links with Phnom Penh.

Foreign ministry spokesman Roy Wu said consideration of Taiwan's "dignity and interests" left Taipei no choice but to withdraw its unofficial representatives from Phnom Penh and order Cambodia's Taipei office closed.

Cambodian strongman Hun Sen on July 22 ordered Taiwan's representative office in Phnom Penh closed, alleging Taiwanese interference in his bloody early July showdown with the forces of royalist co-premier Prince Norodom Ranariddh.
Office chief Chu Che-chuan returned to Taiwan on Sunday.
Taiwan has denied complicity in Cambodia's political turmoil and threatened a drastic response -- including a boycott by Taiwan investors and tourists -- if the closure order stood.
With some US$130 million in Cambodia investments, Taiwan's private sector ranks as the leading source of investment in its unsteady, war-scarred economy.
Taiwan stopped short of calling for a boycott, but said the tit-for-tat office closures would hurt investment.

"In view of Cambodia's unstable political situation and unfriendly attitude, it is impossible for our government to encourage investors to go there," said George Chang, head of the foreign ministry's East Asian affairs department.

Taiwan laid blame for the row squarely with communist China, suggesting Beijing was calling the shots in Phnom Penh and now was widening its longtime diplomatic embargo of what it regards as a renegade province to other non-official spheres.
"Very clearly the Chinese communists are the black hand behind (Cambodia's) barbaric, irrational behaviour," Wu said.
"The reason is simple. The Chinese communists want to clamp down on all our activities in all realms, whether official or unofficial," he said.
Beijing has sought to squeeze Taiwan's exiled Republic of China government off the diplomatic map since it took refuge on the island after its 1949 civil war loss on the mainland.

Because Beijing has rarely opposed the huge economic other unofficial links that Taiwan enjoys with virtually every country on earth, it raised eyebrows on July 24 when it openly welcomed Hun Sen's move against Taiwan's representative office.
Cambodia recognises only Beijing and has no official ties with Taipei.
Hun Sen has encouraged Taiwan people to invest in Cambodia and said Taipei had no need for a Phnom Penh office because they could seek assistance if necessary from Beijing's embassy.

Analysts have said Beijing's support for Hun Sen was surprising in view of China's longtime backing of Hun Sen's rival, Prince Ranariddh, and Ranariddh's father, King Norodom Sihanouk, when they were arrayed against Hun Sen.

In 1979, when China fought a brief border war with Vietnam, the main cause was deep frictions over Hanoi's installation of Hun Sen as a puppet leader in Phnom Penh, where Beijing had long backed the ultraleftist Khmer Rouge.
